answer_text:
Let \(\mu\) be the normalized Haar probability measure on \(K\). For \(x\in K\), write

\[
C_K(x)=\{y\in K: xy=yx\}
\]

for the centralizer of \(x\). Then the probability that two independent Haar-random elements commute is

\[
p=\iint_{K\times K} \mathbf 1_{xy=yx}\,d\mu(x)\,d\mu(y)
   =\int_K \mu(C_K(x))\,d\mu(x).
\]

Now observe the following.

**Lemma.** If \(H\) is a proper closed subgroup of a connected compact group \(G\), then \(\mu_G(H)=0\).

**Proof.** Each left coset \(gH\) is closed. If \(H\) had finite index, then \(G\setminus H\) would be a finite union of closed cosets, hence closed, so \(H\) would be both open and closed. Since \(G\) is connected, a nonempty proper clopen subset is impossible. Therefore a proper closed subgroup has infinite index.

If \(a=\mu_G(H)>0\), then by left invariance every left coset \(gH\) also has measure \(a\). Choosing \(n\) distinct cosets, their union is a Borel subset of \(G\) with measure \(na\), so \(na\le 1\) for all \(n\). Hence \(a=0\). Thus \(\mu_G(H)=0\). \(\square\)

Now apply this to \(K\). For each \(x\in K\), the centralizer \(C_K(x)\) is a closed subgroup. If \(x\) lies in the center \(Z(K)\), then \(C_K(x)=K\), so \(\mu(C_K(x))=1\). If \(x\notin Z(K)\), then \(C_K(x)\) is a proper closed subgroup, so by the lemma \(\mu(C_K(x))=0\). Therefore

\[
p=\int_K \mu(C_K(x))\,d\mu(x)=\mu(Z(K)).
\]

If \(K\) is abelian, then \(Z(K)=K\), so \(p=1\). If \(K\) is non-abelian, then \(Z(K)\) is a proper closed subgroup, so by the lemma \(\mu(Z(K))=0\), and hence \(p=0\).

Thus the commuting probability can never lie strictly between \(0\) and \(1\).

\[
\boxed{\text{No. In fact, }p=1\text{ if }K\text{ is abelian, and }p=0\text{ if }K\text{ is non-abelian.}}
\]
